Listening.transcript:
[Part 1]
You will hear a conversation between a librarian and a new member registering for a library card. First you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10. The new member's surname is spelled Devereaux. The membership category chosen is student. Proof of address must be dated within the last 3 months. The maximum number of books that can be borrowed at once is 8. Loan periods for standard books last 4 weeks. Overdue fines are charged at 20 pence per day. The library's study rooms can be booked via the information desk. The new card will be ready for collection after 2 days. The member's email address ends in ac.uk. Replacement cards cost £3.

[Part 2]
You will hear an announcement about a new community garden scheme. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20. The community garden site covers 24 plots. Plot rental costs £35 per year. Water access is provided from a shared tank. Applications close on the last day of April. New plot holders receive a free bag of compost. The scheme is coordinated by the residents association. Priority for the new plots is given to local residents living within the borough boundary. All plot holders are required to attend a single induction session before receiving their keys. Any plot left unused will be reassigned to another applicant after six months, the coordinator explained. Shared tools are kept in the site office and can be borrowed by any registered plot holder.

[Part 3]
You will hear two students, Ben and Aisha, discussing their recent internships. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30. Ben's internship lasted 10 weeks. Aisha's internship was based at a company with 200 employees. Ben was supervised by a senior manager. Aisha's weekly report was due every Friday. Ben's favourite task involved analysing customer data. Aisha will share her experience at a careers fair next term. Ben explained that his internship was based mainly in the research department, helping with data analysis. Aisha admitted the most challenging part for her was presenting findings to senior staff each week. Both agreed that, above all, the internships had improved their teamwork skills through daily collaboration. Ben said he now plans to apply for a graduate role at the same company after finishing his degree.

[Part 4]
You will hear part of a lecture on the development of written language. First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. The earliest known writing system developed in Mesopotamia. Early writing was primarily used for trade records. Cuneiform script was written on tablets made of clay. The lecturer dates the earliest full sentences in writing to around 2600 BCE. Alphabetic writing systems reduced the number of symbols needed to fewer than 30. The spread of alphabets was greatly helped by trade across the Mediterranean Sea. Movable type printing was developed in China during the eleventh century. The Gutenberg press, introduced in Europe, dramatically increased literacy rates. The lecturer notes that digital text has changed reading habits within the last 20 years. The lecture ends by discussing the future role of natural language processing.

passages.title: The Story of Coffee Cultivation
passages.text: Coffee is now one of the most widely traded agricultural products in the world, yet its cultivation began in a relatively small region and spread only gradually across continents over several centuries. Coffee cultivation is believed to have originated in the highlands of Ethiopia. Coffee was first cultivated as a crop on the Arabian Peninsula around the fifteenth century. Coffeehouses first appeared in cities such as Mecca before spreading to Europe. European traders introduced coffee cultivation to colonies in Java during the seventeenth century. Brazil became the world's largest coffee producer by the nineteenth century. Today, coffee is grown commercially in over 70 countries. Early coffeehouses functioned largely as places for social and intellectual gathering, where news and ideas were exchanged. Brazil's rise was closely linked to its favourable climate and the establishment of large-scale plantations across vast areas of suitable land. passages.title: How Cities Manage Urban Heat
passages.text: As global temperatures rise, city planners are increasingly focused on the urban heat island effect, a phenomenon in which built-up areas become significantly warmer than surrounding rural land. Dense city centres can be up to 7 degrees warmer than nearby countryside at night. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb and re-emit thermal energy. One common mitigation strategy involves painting rooftops a lighter colour. Urban tree cover has been shown to reduce local temperatures by up to 4 degrees. A pilot scheme in one city planted 10000 trees along major roads. Green roofs also help reduce a building's demand for cooling. questions.prompt: The diagram below shows the process of producing bottled drinking water, from source to shelf. Summarise the information by describing the main stages of the process. Write at least 150 words.

stages: Water bottled and sealed on production line
Bottles labelled and packed into crates

questions.modelAnswer:
The diagram illustrates the seven-stage process by which spring water is transformed into bottled drinking water ready for sale.

The process begins with water being extracted directly from a natural spring source. It then passes through a filtration stage designed to remove sediment and larger particles. Following this, the water undergoes ultraviolet treatment, a purification method that eliminates microorganisms without the use of chemicals.

Once purified, samples of the water are sent to a laboratory, where mineral content is tested to ensure it meets quality standards. After passing these checks, the water moves to a production line, where it is bottled and sealed. The sealed bottles are then labelled and packed into crates.

In the final stage, these crates are loaded and transported to distribution centres, from where the bottled water is delivered to retailers. Overall, the process moves in a clear, linear sequence from natural extraction through purification and testing to packaging and distribution.

questions.prompt: In many countries, more people are choosing to work from home rather than commute to an office. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend? Write at least 250 words.
questions.modelAnswer:
The shift toward home-based work, accelerated by recent technological change, brings both clear benefits and notable drawbacks that deserve careful consideration.

Among the advantages, the most obvious is the time and cost saved by eliminating a daily commute. Employees can use this recovered time for rest, family, or personal development, which often improves overall wellbeing. Working from home can also increase flexibility, allowing people to arrange their schedules around personal responsibilities such as childcare, provided their output remains consistent.

However, the disadvantages are equally significant. Many employees report feelings of isolation when working remotely for extended periods, since spontaneous conversations and informal support from colleagues become harder to replicate online. Home working can also blur the boundary between professional and personal life, leading some people to work longer hours than they would in an office, ultimately harming their work-life balance.

Employers, too, face challenges in maintaining company culture and ensuring effective collaboration when teams are physically dispersed. Training new employees remotely, for example, can take considerably longer than in a shared office environment.

In conclusion, while working from home offers valuable flexibility and reduces commuting burdens, it also risks social isolation and blurred boundaries between work and personal life. A hybrid approach, combining office and home working, may offer the most balanced solution for both employees and employers.
